## What M1 is

> **M1 --- Static dashboard (15 pts).** A `flexdashboard` that loads your
> data and displays at least one map and one time series, deployed or
> renderable from your repository.

In the last lecture (*Your First Dashboard*) we built this dashboard on lung
cancer in Ohio. M1 is the same file, on the dataset from your proposal.
Nothing in it is new: the map is the `leaflet` map of Exercise 4, the time
series an ordinary `ggplot`. The work is getting your data in, and telling the
reader clearly what they are looking at.

Your dashboard has three panels:

| Panel | Answers | Part |
|---|---|---|
| a map | *where* | B |
| a time series, or a funnel plot if your data have no time | *when*, or *how far to trust each area* | C |
| About these data | *what, from where, with which limits* | D |

Loading the data (A), the repository (E) and the AI use note (F) complete the
15 points.

::: {.callout-important}
## Before you start
1. Install the packages once, in the **Console**:
   `install.packages(c("flexdashboard", "plotly", "DT"))`.
2. Put your data in the `data/` folder of your course repository.
3. Copy the whole Ohio file (§3.5 of the lecture) into a new file,
   **`dashboard.Rmd`**, at the top of your repository, next to `data/`.
   **Knit it once with the Ohio data before you change anything.** If Ohio
   knits, your setup works, and any later error comes from your data.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Submission
On Course Site, by **Tuesday, November 17, 2026, 11:59 pm**:

1. upload the knitted `dashboard.html`, renamed `LASTNAME_FI_M1.html`;
2. in the text box: the URL of your GitHub repository, the GitHub Pages

- **No expected counts:** map a rate instead (Part B).
- **Point data** (case, facility or crash locations): see *If your data are

- **No time component**, only if we agreed on it: a funnel plot replaces the
  time series (end of Part C).

## Part A --- Your data in the dashboard (3 points)

Change only the setup chunk; the layout stays. As in the lecture, the data are
summarised twice: one row per area for the map, one row per period for the
time series.

| In the Ohio file | For your data |
|---|---|
| `read_csv("data/ohio_lung_cancer_1968_1988.csv", ...)` | your file, with a relative path, `data/...`, never `C:/Users/...` |
| `col_types = cols(GEOID = "c")` | your ID column, as text |
| `counties(state = "OH", ...)` | your state; `tracts()` or `zctas()` for other units |
| `Y`, `E`, `year` | your counts, your expected counts or population, your time column |
| `focus <- "Cuyahoga"` | one area of your data (Part C) |

IDs read as numbers lose their leading zeros: Alabama's Autauga County,
`01001`, becomes `1001`, and the join fails without an error. Pad them back,
as in Exercise 4:

```r
dat <- dat |>
  mutate(GEOID = sprintf("%05d", as.integer(GEOID)))     # counties: 5 digits
# tracts, 11 digits: stringr::str_pad(GEOID, 11, pad = "0")
```

Then run the join check of the lecture, with `rate` in place of `SIR` if you
map a rate:

```
sum(is.na(my_map$SIR))                                   # should be 0
my_map$NAME[is.na(my_map$SIR)]                           # which areas, if not
```

If it is not 0, find out why: a failed join, which you fix, or suppressed
counts, which you report in the About panel (Part D).
```{r}

library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tigris)
library(lubridate)

# 1. Load dataset
raw <- read_csv(
  "data/VSRR_Provisional_County-Level_Drug_Overdose_Death_Counts_20261117.csv",
  col_types = cols(
    FIPS = col_character(),
    `Provisional Drug Overdose Deaths` = col_character(),
    .default = col_guess()
  )
)

# 2. Filter Pennsylvania and clean variables
dat <- raw |>
  filter(ST_ABBREV == "PA") |>
  transmute(
    GEOID = str_pad(FIPS, 5, pad = "0"),
    county = COUNTYNAME,
    month = mdy(MonthEndingDate),
    deaths = parse_number(
      `Provisional Drug Overdose Deaths`
    )
  )

# 3. One row per county for the map
# Use the latest 12-month ending period
latest_month <- max(dat$month)

by_area <- dat |>
  filter(month == latest_month) |>
  select(GEOID, county, cases = deaths)

# 4. One row per month for the time series
by_period <- dat |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarise(
    cases = sum(deaths, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_missing = sum(is.na(deaths)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# 5. Pennsylvania county boundaries
pa_counties <- counties(
  state = "PA",
  cb = TRUE,
  year = 2020,
  progress_bar = FALSE
) |>
  st_transform(4326)

# 6. Join geographic and overdose data
my_map <- pa_counties |>
  left_join(by_area, by = "GEOID")

# 7. Choose focus county for Part C
focus <- "Philadelphia"

focus_series <- dat |>
  filter(county == focus)

# 8. Check missing values
sum(is.na(my_map$cases))

my_map$NAME[is.na(my_map$cases)]

# 9. Check unmatched geographic IDs
anti_join(
  st_drop_geometry(pa_counties),
  by_area,
  by = "GEOID"
)
```

## Part B --- The map (3.5 points)

One `leaflet` map of your measure, for all periods pooled or for the most
recent period; the panel title says which.

**An SIR** keeps the Exercise 4 classes and the red--blue palette of the
lecture, so that the neutral class sits around 1.

**A rate** has no neutral value, so it takes a sequential palette. Pooled over
several years, divide the cases by the population **summed over the years**
(person-years); the result is an average annual rate.

```r
by_area <- dat |>
  group_by(GEOID) |>
  summarise(cases = sum(cases), pop = sum(population), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(rate = 1e5 * cases / pop)                       # per 100,000 person-years

breaks <- quantile(by_area$rate, seq(0, 1, 0.2), na.rm = TRUE)   # quintiles
pal <- colorBin("YlOrRd", domain = by_area$rate, bins = unique(breaks))
```

Then `fillColor = ~pal(rate)` in `addPolygons()`, and
`title = "Rate per 100,000"` in `addLegend()`. `colorBin()` with quintile
breaks, rather than `colorQuantile()`, puts the rates themselves in the legend
instead of percentiles.

**What earns the points:**

- the legend has a title with units;
- the panel title says what, where and when, e.g. *Lung cancer SIR by county,
  Ohio, 1968--1988*;
- the hover label gives the area's name, its value **and the count behind
  it**, so that the reader can tell whether a dark colour rests on many cases
  or on a handful;
- a `>` note under the map says, in one sentence, what the colours mean.

## Part C --- The time series (3.5 points)

One line for the whole study area and one for the area you chose (`focus`),
as in the lecture. With point data, one line of counts per period is enough.

If your periods are months or weeks, make the time column a `Date`
(`as.Date()`, or `lubridate::ym()` for values such as `"2021-03"`), and
`ggplot()` spaces the axis correctly.

**What earns the points:**

- the y-axis names the measure and its units (`labs(y = "Rate per 100,000")`);
- for an SIR, the dashed line at 1 stays;
- the `focus` area has enough cases to be readable: with a handful per year,
  its line jumps up and down and says little, the small-numbers problem of
  Exercise 4;
- a `>` note under the panel says, in one sentence, what the series shows: a
  rise, a fall, a peak, or no clear change.

`ggplotly(p)` (hover, zoom) is welcome but not required.

### If your data have no time component

Check first: many sources publish one release per year (CDC WONDER can group
by year; County Health Rankings and CDC PLACES publish yearly releases). Three
or four years are enough for a time series, and M2 and M3 build on one.

If your data really cover a single period, and we agreed on it, replace the
time series with a **funnel plot**: each area's value against its size. The
map shows *where* values are high; the funnel plot shows *which of them rest
on enough cases to take seriously*, the small-numbers problem of Exercise 4.
By chance alone, the SIR of an area with $E$ expected cases varies by about
$1/\sqrt{E}$, so the band of chance variation narrows as $E$ grows.

```r
d <- st_drop_geometry(my_map) |>
  filter(!is.na(SIR))                                    # areas with data

# 95% limits around SIR = 1 (normal approximation)
funnel <- tibble(E = 10^seq(log10(min(d$E)), log10(max(d$E)),
                            length.out = 100)) |>
  mutate(lo = pmax(0, 1 - 1.96 / sqrt(E)),
         hi = 1 + 1.96 / sqrt(E))

p <- ggplot(d, aes(E, SIR)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(data = funnel, aes(y = lo), linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(data = funnel, aes(y = hi), linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(text = NAME), colour = "#B2182B") +     # text: hover label
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Expected cases (log scale)", y = "SIR") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p, tooltip = c("text", "x", "y"))               # hover, zoom
```

With a rate, centre the funnel on the overall rate, with the population on
the x-axis:

```r
d <- st_drop_geometry(my_map) |>
  filter(!is.na(rate))                                   # areas with data

r0 <- sum(d$cases) / sum(d$pop)                          # overall rate
funnel <- tibble(pop = 10^seq(log10(min(d$pop)), log10(max(d$pop)),
                              length.out = 100)) |>
  mutate(lo = 1e5 * pmax(0, r0 - 1.96 * sqrt(r0 / pop)),
         hi = 1e5 * (r0 + 1.96 * sqrt(r0 / pop)))
# then aes(pop, rate), yintercept = 1e5 * r0, x = "Population (log scale)"
```

The limits are approximate, and rough below about 10 expected cases. About one
area in 20 falls outside 95% limits by chance alone, so a point outside the
funnel is worth a second look, not yet a finding. With point data and no time,
see *If your data are points*, below.

**What earns the points** for the funnel plot: labelled axes with units; the
reference line and the 95% limits; hover labels with the area's name; a `>`
note saying which areas lie outside the funnel, and whether they are the
darkest areas on the map.

## If your data are points

One row per event (a case, a facility, a crash) with its coordinates and,
ideally, a date. The layout stays; Parts A to D change as follows.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Private locations
If each point is a person, such as a case at a home address, the points stay
on your laptop. Do not push them to GitHub: in GitHub Desktop, right-click the
data file under **Changes** and choose **Ignore file**. Do not upload the
knitted dashboard either, since it contains the coordinates: upload
`dashboard.Rmd` only, and show me the dashboard on your laptop. Facilities,
crashes and audits are not private and follow the usual rules.
:::

**A. Read the points.** There are no boundaries to join: the coordinates
become an `sf` object. The boundaries only outline the study area.

```r
raw <- read_csv("data/my_points.csv")
pts <- raw |>
  filter(!is.na(lon), !is.na(lat)) |>                    # rows with coordinates
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)         # longitude first
nrow(raw) - nrow(pts)                                    # rows dropped

area <- counties(state = "PA", cb = TRUE, year = 2020,
                 progress_bar = FALSE) |>
  filter(NAME %in% c("Lehigh", "Northampton")) |>        # your study area
  st_transform(4326)
```

Unlike SaTScan's coordinates file in Exercise 6, `coords` takes **longitude
first**. Swapped, Pennsylvania lands in Antarctica. Coordinates in metres or
feet, such as a state plane, take that system's EPSG code in `crs =`, followed
by `st_transform(4326)`.

**B. The map.** Circles in place of polygons, with the study area outlined so
that the reader sees where there are no points:

```r
leaflet(pts) |>
  addProviderTiles("CartoDB.Positron") |>
  addPolygons(data = area, fill = FALSE, color = "grey40", weight = 1) |>
  addCircleMarkers(radius = 4, stroke = FALSE, fillOpacity = 0.6,
                   color = "#B2182B", label = ~as.character(date))
```

The label describes the point (its date, its type), never a name or an
address. With thousands of points, add
`clusterOptions = markerClusterOptions()` to `addCircleMarkers()`; the
numbered bubbles count nearby points and are not statistical clusters. Points
coloured by a category (`colorFactor()`) need a legend.

A point map has no denominator. Dense points mostly mark where many people
live, or where the facilities are, as with complete spatial randomness in
Exercise 3: the `>` note under the map says so.

**C. The time series.** Counts per period, as bars:

```r
by_month <- pts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(date)) |>
  count(month = lubridate::floor_date(date, "month"))    # cases per month

p <- ggplot(by_month, aes(month, n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#B2182B") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Cases per month") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)                                              # hover, zoom
```

`floor_date()` also takes `"week"` or `"year"`. Bars rather than a line: a
month without cases has no row, and a line would join across it. Without a
population, a rise in counts may come from more people, more testing or better
reporting rather than higher risk; the note under the panel says what the bars
show, with that caution.

**No dates?** Replace the time series with a kernel density map of the points,
as in Exercise 3:

```r
xy <- st_transform(pts, 5070)                            # metres
ggplot() +
  stat_density_2d_filled(data = as.data.frame(st_coordinates(xy)),
                         aes(X, Y), contour_var = "ndensity", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_sf(data = st_transform(area, 5070), fill = NA, colour = "grey30") +
  labs(fill = "Relative density") +
  theme_void()
```

The bandwidth here follows a default rule; in M2, a slider can hand it to the
reader. The note under the panel says where the density peaks, and whether
that is more than where people live.

**D. About these data.** State that there is no population at risk, so the
maps show counts, not risk; how the locations were obtained (GPS, geocoded
addresses); and how many rows were dropped for missing coordinates.

**What earns the points** with point data: in B, the study area outlined,
labels that identify no one, a legend if the points are coloured, a title with
what, where and when, and the note on the missing denominator; in C, the
y-axis as counts per period (or the density legend), and a note on what the
panel shows.

## Part D --- About these data (2 points)

A third panel, in plain text, with no R code. Most of it comes from your
dataset proposal. For Ohio:

````markdown
### About these data

- **Outcome:** lung cancer cases, 1968--1988, by year.
- **Population at risk:** residents of Ohio's 88 counties.
- **Expected counts:** indirect standardization by age and sex.
- **Source:** Moraga (2019), Ch. 7; boundaries from the US Census Bureau, via `tigris`.
- **Areas without data:** none.
- **Limitation:** the expected counts use one set of rates for the whole
  period, so the map averages over the rise in lung cancer.
````

Put it in the second column, under the time series, in place of the table.
To keep the table as well, give the About panel a third column of its own,
with one more line `Column {data-width=300}` followed by a line of dashes.

**What earns the points:** the outcome and period; the population at risk and
the geography (unit and number of areas); how the expected counts or the rate
were computed; the source, with a link if there is one; the areas without data
(Part A); and **one limitation** of your data, such as suppressed small counts,
missing years or boundary changes. Your final dashboard has to state these
limits in the app itself, so this panel carries over.

## Part E --- Renderable from your repository (2 points)

1. The YAML header keeps `source_code: embed`: I read your code from the
   **Source Code** button of the dashboard.
2. **Session > Restart R**, then **Knit**. Not `quarto render`, which turns the
   dashboard into a scrolling page. It must knit from a clean start.
3. Commit and push `dashboard.Rmd` **and your data** with GitHub Desktop. If
   your data cannot go on GitHub (a file over 50 MB, or data you may not
   share), push a script that downloads them, or email me how to obtain them.

**Publishing to GitHub Pages is optional** and earns the same credit (§3.7 of
the lecture: two entries in `_quarto.yml`). It is worth doing: the Shiny
version you build for M2 cannot run on GitHub Pages, so this is the version of
your dashboard that others can open.

If Knit fails on your laptop, use a lab machine or
[Posit Cloud](https://posit.cloud). If it fails everywhere, push the file
anyway and email me the exact error message: partial work earns partial
credit. The tables *Before you demonstrate M1* and *When it breaks* at the end
of the lecture cover most problems.

## Part F --- AI use note (1 point)

Two or three sentences in the text box of your submission: **which** tools you
used, **what** for, and at **which stage** (planning, coding, debugging,
interpreting, writing). No amount of disclosed use costs points.

## Points

| Part | What earns the points | Points |
|---|---|---|
| A | Data read with a relative path; ID kept as text; join check at 0, or the missing areas explained; one summary per area and one per period | 3 |
| B | Map of your measure with a palette suited to it; legend with title and units; panel title with what, where and when; hover label with name, value and count; note on the colours | 3.5 |
| C | Study area and one chosen area over time; y-axis with units; reference line at 1 for an SIR; readable `focus` area; note on what the series shows. Without time: funnel plot with its limits, hover labels and note | 3.5 |
| D | Outcome, population, geography, method, source, areas without data, one limitation | 2 |
| E | `dashboard.Rmd` and data (or a download script) pushed; knits from a clean session; `source_code: embed` | 2 |
| F | AI use note | 1 |
| | **Total** | **15** |

With point data, Parts B and C are graded on the criteria in *If your data
are points*.

A reader who has never seen your data should understand each panel without
asking you. Clear titles and notes earn as many points as the code.
